planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Blake's Pride was bred specifically for strong fire blight resistance and performs well in humid climates where European pears normally struggle with the disease.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing trees to allow good air circulation through the canopy to further limit blight pressure. Blake's Pride was released by USDA breeders working out of the Appalachian Fruit Research Station in West Virginia specifically to combine strong fire blight resistance with genuinely good dessert quality, producing a Seckel-type fruit that is sweeter and larger than old Seckel itself. Plant it alongside another mid-season European pear such as Moonglow or Magness for reliable cross-pollination. Pick the fruit while still firm in late summer and let it finish ripening indoors at room temperature for the best texture and flavor.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service pear breeding program

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Potomac is a fire-blight-resistant Bartlett-type selection well suited to humid Southeastern growing conditions.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and prune out any blighted shoots well below visible discoloration as soon as they appear. Potomac came out of the same USDA fire blight resistance breeding effort that produced Blake's Pride and Sunrise, and it is valued for producing a larger, more Bartlett-like fruit than most of the other resistant selections from that program, with good flavor for fresh eating and canning. Give it a compatible mid-season pollinizer, since it is only partially self-fruitful. Harvest while the fruit is still hard and green-yellow, then ripen it indoors for the best dessert texture.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service pear breeding program

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter; Sunrise is an early-ripening, fire-blight-resistant European pear, a good option for gardeners in humid regions who want to beat blight pressure with an earlier harvest.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and site the tree with good air movement to keep humidity around the foliage down. Sunrise is one of the earliest-ripening pears to come out of the USDA's fire blight resistance program, producing a small to medium yellow fruit with soft, juicy flesh well ahead of Bartlett and most other European pears. That early harvest window is a real practical advantage in humid climates, since the tree spends less of the growing season vulnerable to blight infection during active shoot growth. Pick fruit while still firm and ripen it indoors, and pair it with another early to mid-season pear for pollination.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service pear breeding program

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; White Doyenne is an old, historically important European dessert pear, grown in America since colonial times under the name Virgalieu.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinizer for best fruit set. White Doyenne was, for generations before Bartlett rose to dominance, the standard dessert pear of American and European gardens, prized for smooth, melting, richly flavored flesh on a small to medium yellow fruit often blushed with red. It is more susceptible to fire blight and pear scab than modern resistant releases, so it suits growers more interested in preserving a genuinely historic variety than in low-maintenance production. Pick the fruit while still firm in early to mid fall and ripen it indoors at room temperature for the best flavor and texture.
sources: Cornell University historic fruit variety archives

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; Highland is a Bartlett-type Pacific Northwest selection valued for heavy, reliable production.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, training young trees to an open-center or modified central-leader form for strong scaffold branches under a heavy crop load. Highland originated as a selection out of the Pacific Northwest pear industry and is grown as a productive, dependable alternative to straight Bartlett, ripening slightly later with firmer, longer-keeping flesh that holds up well in storage and shipping. It shares Bartlett's classic bell shape and greenish-yellow skin, and performs best with a mid-season pollinizer such as Anjou or Bosc nearby. Harvest while still hard and green, then ripen indoors at room temperature for the best dessert texture.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; Colette is a compact, self-fertile French pear bred for disease tolerance and small-garden use, so a second pollinizer is helpful but not required.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Colette's naturally compact, upright growth habit makes it a practical choice for a small yard or large container where a full-size pear tree would not fit. Bred in France with an emphasis on tolerance to common pear diseases as well as self-fertility, it will set a crop as a single tree, though fruiting is heavier with another European pear blooming nearby. The fruit is medium-sized with the classic sweet, juicy dessert flavor typical of French pear breeding programs. Prune lightly in winter mainly to keep the naturally tidy form open to light and air.
sources: European nursery trade catalogs and INRA fruit breeding program references
